one_liner: Zero-dependency Rust CommonMark parser shipped as SIMD WebAssembly; replaces remark-parse and beats JS markdown renderers in Node.
what_it_does: Parses all of CommonMark 0.31.2 (652/652 spec examples) to HTML, with GFM and other extensions as opt-in Cargo features, and optionally to an mdast tree that deep-equals mdast-util-from-markdown including positions. The npm package @momiji-rs/sparkdown exposes toHtml/toHtmlSync (pure, /gfm and /full bundles) and a /mdast subpath that is a unified parser plugin, so a unified/remark/rehype pipeline can swap remark-parse for it; the Rust crate exposes to_html / to_html_with and, behind the ast feature, to_mdast.
how_it_is_fast: A port of cmark's incremental block algorithm over zero-copy borrowed slices, SIMD byte-set matchers (simdjson-style nibble lookup on NEON/SSE, wasm v128 kernels) that skip plain text to the next significant byte, a fused SIMD HTML escaper, an intrusive first-child/next-sibling node tree and a bump arena. For mdast it builds the tree in wasm and ships it to JS as a compact binary wire format (string-pooled when positions are off) that is read into plain objects without JSON.parse.
when_to_use: unified/remark/rehype pipelines in Node, Bun, Deno or edge runtimes where remark-parse dominates build time and plugins only walk the tree
Rendering CommonMark or GFM to HTML in JavaScript hosts that would otherwise use markdown-it or marked, with cmark-identical output
Non-JS hosts (wasmtime, wazero, Workers) that want a self-contained, WASI-free markdown .wasm module with a raw C-ABI
Native Rust code that wants a dependency-free CommonMark renderer about as fast as pulldown-cmark (0.59 vs 0.68 ms on the 198 KB spec, first-party)
when_not_to_use: Native Rust users already on pulldown-cmark who need its event/iterator API or ecosystem: sparkdown's lead there is about 1.15x and its wasm build is slower than native pulldown-cmark

remark pipelines that rely on syntax-extension plugins hooking micromark (math, MDX and similar): parsing happens in wasm, so only the extensions compiled into sparkdown (GFM, footnotes, frontmatter, directives, definition lists, emoji) are available
Hosts without WebAssembly SIMD support: the documented wasm build enables +simd128 and +bulk-memory
Synchronous use on the browser main thread: initSync throws there because synchronous wasm compilation is capped at about 4 KB; use the async init
Teams that need a maintained, widely reviewed parser: v0.1.0, 3 stars, 145 crates.io downloads (npm about 46k per month per the verifier's registry search), no commits since 2026-06-27

integration.form: crate (rlib + cdylib) + npm module (ESM, wasm base64-inlined, four subpath bundles) + raw .wasm with a C-ABI
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.95, edition 2024; npm package declares Node >=18
integration.platforms: any Rust target (SIMD paths on NEON/SSE, SWAR fallback); wasm32-unknown-unknown with simd128 + bulk-memory for Node, browsers, Deno, Bun and edge runtimes
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — /mdast is a drop-in unified parser plugin for remark-parse (deep-equal on the 652 CommonMark examples including position, per README) but not for micromark syntax extensions; the HTML API is not API-compatible with markdown-it or marked

gotchas: Harness flaw: the README's JS table (sparkdown wasm 0.90 ms vs markdown-it 4.52 ms and marked 5.20 ms) has no benchmark in the repo; harness/package.json depends on neither markdown-it nor marked, and their versions and options (markdown-it preset, html flag) are not stated, so the 5.0x/5.7x rows cannot be reproduced.

Harness flaw: harness/nopos_bench.mjs times sparkdown_to_mdast_wire_nopos_opts through an inline-string reader written in the harness (best of 20 batches of 25), while the published npm toMdast({position:false}) calls sparkdown_to_mdast_wire_fast_opts with a string-pooled reader, and the harness wasm is built with ast,wasm while the npm /mdast bundle is ast,full; the README's ~0.9 ms 'best-of-15' row therefore does not come from a script that runs the shipped entry point. The ~80x headline also pairs the no-position tree with remark, which always builds positions; like-for-like it is ~1.9 vs ~73 ms (~38x, derived from page data).

Only sparkdown vs pulldown-cmark is benchmarked in-repo (benches/vs_pulldown.rs, criterion); the rushdown, comrak, markdown-rs and cmark rows have no harness, cmark was compared CLI-to-CLI on a 16 MB document, and the wasm rows (measured in Node) sit in the same table as native in-process times.

Output is not cmark-identical in every case: the README lists fuzz-found differences (native to_html keeps a trailing tab at the end of a block where cmark strips it; mdast value of indented code with trailing blank lines keeps one fewer newline than remark; a nested blockquote closed by '>\t' over-extends by a line).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against markdown-wasm and md4w (md4c compiled to wasm, also beating markdown-it), pick sparkdown when you need an mdast tree for the unified/remark ecosystem or GFM/extension bundles behind one API; for plain HTML rendering the three have not been measured on the same run, so md4c-based packages remain the more established choice.
verified_claims_summary: First-party, one Apple Mac Studio (chip not stated), 198 KB CommonMark spec: native sparkdown renders HTML in 0.59 ms against pulldown-cmark's 0.68 ms (criterion, in-repo), the wasm build in 0.90-0.93 ms in Node against markdown-it 4.52 ms and marked 5.20 ms (no in-repo harness), and the wasm mdast path builds a fully materialised tree in ~1.9 ms with positions against ~73 ms for mdast-util-from-markdown (~38x; ~0.9 ms without positions).
status_note: MIT, zero dependencies and small, but a two-week burst of work (0.0.1 to 0.1.0 between 2026-06-24 and 2026-06-27) with no commits since and no open issues; treat it as an unproven young release rather than an actively maintained project.
